references.text: The priests who approach the Lord must consecrate themselves, so that the Lord does not break out against them. This illustrates the same principle of holiness for those who come near to God (בִּקְרֹבַי אֶקָּדֵשׁ).
The Lord says he will meet with the children of Israel there, and the place shall be made holy by his glory. This connects God's nearness with his holiness.
The priests must be holy to their God and not profane the name of their God, for they present the Lord's fire offerings. It emphasizes the requirement of holiness for those who serve near God.

Moses and Aaron did not honor the Lord in the sight of the children of Israel, and therefore were not allowed to lead the people into the land. This shows the consequence of failing to hallow God before the people (וְעַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָעָם אֶכָּבֵד).
The Lord will show himself great and holy, making himself known in the sight of many peoples. The same theme that God hallows himself and is honored before the people.
The Lord shall be hallowed among those who come near him, and he shall be honored before all the people. A direct parallel to the words in Leviticus 10:3.
Job was silent and opened not his mouth, like Aaron who kept silence (וַיִּדֹּם אַהֲרֹן) in his grief and submission under God's judgment.
Be still and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations. This links silence with recognition of God's majesty and glory.
Judgment begins at the house of God. This shows that God holds his own people and servants to a higher standard of holiness.
We must serve God with reverence, for our God is a consuming fire. A parallel to the seriousness of approaching the holy God.
